Descriptive Statistics 3: Measures of Dispersion

Introduction

Welcome back! Our journey into Descriptive Statistics continues with Measures of Dispersion.

These measures, which include the range, interquartile range, variance, and standard deviation, inform us about the extent to which our data is spread. R’s built-in statistical functions offer all we need to measure and understand dispersion in our data. Let’s dive right in!

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Define and understand four common measures of dispersion: range, interquartile range, variance, and standard deviation.
  2. Compute these statistics in R using the functions range(), IQR(), var(), and sd().
  3. Use {ggplot2} functions to visualize the distribution of a numeric variable, with markers for the mean and standard deviation.

Measures of Dispersion

Measures of Dispersion capture the spread within a dataset. For example, knowing the average height (a Measure of Centrality) isn’t enough. Understanding how those heights vary from the average provides a fuller picture. This enhanced comprehension is vital for daily data analysis.

In this diagram, you can see three levels of dispersion in these distributions:

We could qualitatively assess the amount of variability in these curves by visual inspection. We can see that there’s a data distribution with low dispersion (green), medium dispersion (red), and high dispersion (blue). But what if we want a quantitative measurement that can give us a specific number to describe the amount of dispersion?

Three common measures of dispersion are:

  • Range

  • Variance

  • Standard Deviation

TipDefining Measures of Dispersion

Measures of dispersion are statistics that capture the spread or variation of a data distribution. They describe the extent to which the values of a variable are different.

The most common measures of dispersion are range, variance, and standard deviation.

TipRecap: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

Both Measures of Dispersion and Central Tendency are numbers that are used to describe various parameters of continuous data. Let’s see the differences between Measures of Dispersion and Central Tendency.

Central Tendency Measure of Dispersion
Numerically describe the center or typical values of a data distribution | Numerically quantify the variability or spread

Common measures of central tendency:

Mean

Median

Mode

Common measures of dispersion:

Range & IQR

Variance

Standard Deviation

In the last lesson on measures of central tendency, we found the mean value, median value, mode value, of the height variable in our yaounde dataset.

Earlier, we also created boxplots to visualize the maximum and minimum values of the height_cm variable, as well as the quartile ranges. This is a graphical summary of dispersion – can we put a number to it this time?

In short, Measures of Dispersion allow us to mathematically quantify and measure the level of dispersion.

Load Packages

This lesson will require the following packages to be installed and loaded:

# Load packages 
if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, 
               here,
               DescTools)

pacman::p_load_current_gh("the-graph-courses/inspectdf")

The Yaounde COVID-19 dataset

In this lesson, we will again use the data from the COVID-19 serological survey conducted in Yaounde, Cameroon.

# Import data to RStudio
yaounde_raw <- read_csv(here("data/yaounde_data.csv"))

The survey estimated how many people had been infected with COVID-19 in the region, by testing for IgG and IgM antibodies. The full dataset can be obtained from Zenodo, and the paper can be viewed here.

Spend some time browsing through this dataset. Each line corresponds to one patient surveyed. There are some demographic, socio-economic and COVID-related variables. The results of the IgG and IgM antibody tests are in the columns igg_result and igm_result.

In the last lesson we did some data cleaning to convert variables to the correct type. Let’s copy and rerun that code to clean the raw data.

# Clean and transform variables (copy code from previous lesson)

yaounde <- yaounde_raw %>%  
  mutate(across(starts_with("is_drug"), as.logical),
         across(starts_with("n_"), as.integer),
         age_category_3 = factor(age_category_3,
                                 levels = c("Child",
                                            "Adult",
                                            "Senior")), 
         is_smoker = factor(is_smoker,
                            levels = c("Non-smoker",
                                       "Ex-smoker",
                                       "Smoker")),
         highest_education = factor(highest_education,
                                    levels = c(
                            "No formal instruction",
                            "Primary",
                            "Secondary",
                            "University",
                            "Doctorate",
                            "No response"))
         )

Visually inspect variable types:

inspect_types(yaounde) %>% show_plot()

Next we will calculate the range, variance and standard deviation using the height_cm variable as an example.

  • Range: Maximum value - Minimum value

  • Quartiles:

    • 25% of values lie below the lower quartile (Q1)

    • 25% of values lie above the upper quartile (Q3)

  • Interquartile Range: Q3 - Q1 (50% of values lie in this range)

  • Variance & Standard Deviation - Measure of difference between each observation and the mean

All these measures can be calculated using the inspect_num() function:

# Summary statistics of numeric variables in yaounde
num_sum_yao <- inspect_num(yaounde)

num_sum_yao

However, we want to learn the individual R functions for each measure.

R functions for common measures of dispersion:

  • Range - range()

  • Interquartile Range - IQR()

  • Variance - var()

  • Standard Deviation - sd()

For the remaining calculations, let’s use a subset of just adult men from Yaounde, because we found that men’s heights are much more normally distributed.

# Heights of patients from the Yaounde dataset as a numeric vector
height_men <- yaounde %>% 
  filter(sex == "Male",
         age_category_3 == "Adult") %>% 
  pull(height_cm)

Range

Range is a very simple statistic, as it is simply the difference between the maximum and minimum values in the data.

Calculating Range in R

The range, simply the difference between the highest and lowest values, illustrates the spread between the extremes of our dataset. We can calculate the range of a set of numbers using R’s built-in function, range(). Here, we calculate the range of heights in our data subset:

# The range() function gives us the minimum and maximum values
range(height_men)
[1] 147 196
# Calculate the range
diff(range(height_men))
[1] 49

Range is not very useful from a statistical standpoint; because it relies only on the outermost values of a dataset, two datasets with the same range could still have drastic differences in their overall distribution.

Interquartile Range (IQR)

Finding the quartiles of a given dataset is simple with the R quantile() function.

# Print quantiles
quantile(height_men)
  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
 147  168  172  177  196

IQR is the difference between the 25th and 75th percentiles.

# IQR function
IQR(height_men)
[1] 9

Recall that the “box” part of a box-and-whisker plot (a.k.a. boxplot) extends from Q1 to Q3, visualizing the interquartile range.

The “whiskers” are calculated with the formula \(Q1 - 1.5 \times IQR\) for the lower whisker and \(Q3 + 1.5 \times IQR\) for the upper whisker.

NotePractice

Use the yaounde dataframe. Write R code to compute the interquartile range (IQR) of the weight_kg column.

Variance

Variance, another Measure of Dispersion, quantifies the degree to which data values differ from the mean.

High variance signifies that data points are spread out, while low variance indicates closeness.

Variance is defined as the average of the squared differences from the mean.

Variance shows how much the numbers in your data vary from the average value.

  • If the variance is small, the numbers are close to the mean.
  • If the variance is large, the numbers are more spread out.

Calculating Variance in R

We can calculate the variance using R’s built-in var() function:

# Calculate the variance
var(height_men)
[1] 50.04607

The output helps us understand the level of variability from the average.

# Calculate the variance of everyone in the dataset
var(yaounde$height_cm)
[1] 352.5515

The variation in height in the whole dataset is around 7 times greater than the variation in height of adult men. The full dataset includes children and women, who have a larger range of heights than just the adult men.

Standard Deviation

Rooted in Variance, the Standard Deviation is the square root of the Variance. It measures how much each data point differs from the mean or average.

A low Standard Deviation means values are close to the average, while a high standard deviation means values spread out over a wider range.

NotePractice

Which of the following statements best describes the standard deviation?

  1. It measures the highest value minus the lowest value in a dataset.
  2. It is the square of the mean.
  3. It quantifies the average distance of data points from the mean.
  4. It is always larger than the variance.

Calculating Standard Deviation in R

We can compute it using the sd() function available in R.

# Calculate the standard deviation
sd(height_men)
[1] 7.074325
NotePractice

Which of these R functions correctly calculates the variance of a numeric vector?

  1. range()
  2. sd()
  3. var()
  4. mean()

Visualizing Mean, Variance, and Standard Deviation Together

Here we are going to use {ggplot2} code to create a density plot of height_cm, and overlay the mean, standard deviation, and variance on the plot.

The final plot should look like this:

First, let’s store the key statistics we want to plot.

# Calculate mean, variance, and standard deviation
mean_value <- mean(height_men)
variance_value <- var(height_men)
sd_value <- sd(height_men)

Now, we create a density plot using geom_density(), add vertical lines using geom_vline(), and annotations using the annotate() function.

# Create the plot with variance annotation
yaounde %>% 
  filter(sex == "Male",
         age_category_3 == "Adult") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = height_cm)) +
  # Density plot
  geom_density(fill = "dodgerblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  # Mean line
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_value), color = "indianred", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
   # SD line (right)
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_value + sd_value), color = "forestgreen", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1) + 
   # SD line (left)
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_value - sd_value), color = "forestgreen", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Visualization of Mean, Variance, and Standard Deviation",
       x = "Height",
       y = "Relative Frequency") +
  annotate("text", x = mean_value, y = 0.04, label = paste("Mean =", round(mean_value, 2)), color = "indianred", vjust = -1) + 
  # SD labels positioned at ± 2*sd_value for readability
  annotate("text", x = mean_value + 2*sd_value, y = 0.02, label = paste("Mean + 1 SD =", round(mean_value + sd_value, 2)), color = "forestgreen", vjust = -1) +
  annotate("text", x = mean_value - 2*sd_value, y = 0.02, label = paste("Mean - 1 SD =", round(mean_value - sd_value, 2)), color = "forestgreen", vjust = -1) +
  annotate("text", x = 190, y = 0.05, label = paste("Variance =", round(variance_value, 2)), color = "blue", vjust = -1)

Conclusion

Great job! You’ve just dived into Measures of Dispersion with R! These skills will assist you in better interpreting and visualizing data. Most importantly, the standard deviation is a crucial statistical measure that provides valuable information about the variability or dispersion of data within a dataset. It helps us understand how spread out the data points are from the mean, offering a clearer picture of the data’s consistency and reliability. It is widely used in various fields, including statistics, finance, and science, to understand the distribution of data and make informed decisions based on the level of variability present.

Answer Key

Practice 1: Interquartile Range of weight_kg

Use the yaounde dataframe. Write R code to compute the interquartile range (IQR) of the weight_kg column.

IQR(yaounde$weight_kg, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 27
# Equivalent tidyverse approach:
yaounde %>% pull(weight_kg) %>% IQR(na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 27

Practice 2: Defining Standard Deviation

Which of the following statements best describes the standard deviation?

  1. It measures the highest value minus the lowest value in a dataset.
  2. It is the square of the mean.
  3. It quantifies the average distance of data points from the mean.
  4. It is always larger than the variance.

Answer: C) It quantifies the average distance of data points from the mean.

A describes the range. B is incorrect, the standard deviation is the square root of the variance, not related to the square of the mean. D is false, since for variance values less than 1, the standard deviation is actually larger, but for variance values greater than 1, the standard deviation is smaller, so the relationship is not fixed.

Practice 3: R Function for Variance

Which of these R functions correctly calculates the variance of a numeric vector?

  1. range()
  2. sd()
  3. var()
  4. mean()

Answer: C) var()

range() returns the minimum and maximum, sd() computes the standard deviation, and mean() computes the arithmetic mean.
